content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new GNN for classifying chemical molecule graphs by enriching nodes with predefined motifs. It seems to be a good idea to have motif information in molecules and the paper does implement one way of encoding them.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ The objective of enriching nodes/molecules with motif information deserves investigation and paper shows one way to do that. 
+ The method seems to enhance usual graph neural networks by having more extracted features to the nodes. 
- I think that the way of comparing node neighborhood with motifs is primitive and expensive. 
- From they way motif features are defined, I can't help asking why usual graph mining techniques that search for exact motif appearance on molecules are not deployed?
- By encoding motifs into node features, there might be problem that a motif does appear in the molecules by poorly recognized by any node. This could be the case of a long motif. I'm guessing that the paper might do well with more "local" motifs.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper is clear very clear in presentation and writing and deliver the message well. 
- Novelty of the method is limited, but the idea is valid.
- It looks like it can be reproduced without too much difficulty.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think having motif information is a good point of the paper while the method isn't too novel nor efficient.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors tackle the problem of molecular graph processing with connectionist architecture by proposing additional node features based on the similarity to cluster representatives.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Good:
Graph neural networks are known to suffer from oversmoothing and approaches to compensate these issues are welcome. 

Bad:
The idea is quite simple and it is not adequately tested against significative baselines. 
In practice the authors propose to extract small neighbourhood  subgraphs, cluster them, select a representative from each cluster, and augment the node attributes with a vector that encodes the <<similarity scores between the subgraph of the node and all motifs>>. The authors propose their own notion of similarity. 
The idea of augmenting nodes with the distance/similarity  to cluster centres is not new. 

For a significative baseline comparison, the authors  should compare an original way to assess the subgraph similarity (best would be if end-to-end trainable) with some of the already established graph kernels (path based kernels, tree based kernels, graphlet based kernels, etc).
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea is simply to augment the node attribute with the distance/simlarity  wrt subgraph representatives  (obtained via offline clustering).
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an unsupervised motif-based node feature encoder with nice properties to benefit MPNN-like architectures in molecular property prediction tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength

- This paper proposes an unsupervised feature encoder which is less sensitive to graph size, node 3D position rotation, and node 3D position translatation, which can boost generlization power of MPNN-like architecture for molecolar property prediction.
- Proposed feature encoder is an unsupervised preprocessing method which can be plugged into any MPNN-like archirectures.
- Empirical results show that there method is capable of improving performance of MPNN-like architectures in real-world tasks.

## Weakness

Experiments can not precisely validate conclusions.

- The synethetic task is only used to test size sensitivity (adding nodes) and feature noise sensitivity (adding Gaussian noise). However, I think the benefit of proposed method also includes insensitivity to rotation and translation, explicit synthetic test of these two is missing which is fatal.
- GCN, GAT, GIN is not good method for size insensitivity, and there is method which is less sensitive to size, e.g., I can quickly find [1]. It will be better to use these methods as your synthetic baselines. Besides, I can not believe that GAT, GIN, GCN is the state-of-the-art for graph-level classification. Thus, I will expect more state-of-the-art baselines fitting your scenario rather than just these generic methods.
- It is necessary to show node embedding t-SNE of other baselines. For example, it is possible that CF3 inputs are all similar, thus any method will map them to nearly the same embedding; CH2OH inputs only has two significant different environment, thus any method will map them into two clusters. Current result can not validate that your method has good explanability.
- Why Table 3 has no confidence interval? Some improvement is not significant, e.g., ZPVE. It will be better to report confidence interval to verify concrete improvement.

[1] Bevilacqua, Beatrice, Yangze Zhou, and Bruno Ribeiro. "Size-invariant graph representations for graph classification extrapolations." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a novel procedure to generate "substructural motif aware" initial node features for subsequent GNN learning. First, a set of motif vocabulary (a set of motif subgraphs) is constructed by sampling subgraphs (e.g., k-hop neighborhoods) from the dataset,  clustering them by hierarchical clustering, and selecting representative subgraphs as motifs from each cluster. Then, the newly designed Motif Convolution Module (MCM) computes the normalized similarity between every motif and the subgraph centered at each node, and the vector of all similarity scores to motifs is used as a node feature vector for subsequent GNN message passing (optionally, this vector can be fed into MLPs before they are fed into GNNs). Adding this "preceding" step to standard GNNs such as GCN and GIN makes GNNs more substructural-motif aware and improves the prediction performance in molecular graph classification and regression tasks. MCM is based on computing graph matching between motifs and node-centered subgraphs, which is an NP-hard problem in general, so the paper also develops an efficient suboptimal algorithm and further acceleration with GPUs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strength]

- The main idea of computing similarities between prepared motifs and subgraphs centered at each node and using it as initial node features for subsequent GNNs are novel as far as I know, and very interesting to see if this simple idea worked. For the simple synthetic data case, MCM + logistic regressor without any GNN updates in between was already better than simply applying GCN, GIN, and GAT.

- One of the technical challenges of this approach would be the point that computing similarities between graphs is computationally hard in general. This paper develops a suboptimal algorithm for graph matching computation as well as some engineering effort to implement GPU acceleration.

- The paper provided interesting empirical evaluation: 1) synthetic dataset, 2) 2D GNN tasks (MoleculeNet), 3) 3D geometric GNN tasks (QM9). 1) is the interesting, specific case where MCM+head regressor without GNNs was better than standard GNNs. 2) and 3) demonstrate that this motif-awareness worked well both in 2D cases (just combinatorial) and 3D cases (with the geometry of xyz coordinates).

[Weaknesses]

- The section "2.1 motif vocabulary construction" was a bit ambiguous and unclear to me. Roughly I think I could understand the idea, but this part should be one of the core parts of this paper, and it should have been more concrete.    
   
The most unclear part is how to select "representative subgraphs" from clustering results of subgraphs sampled from the given dataset. Because these are graphs, picking up a single representative is far from trivial (this can cause another NP-hard computation). Furthermore, these selected subgraphs are used as reference motifs for graph matching of MCM and thus, this selection would impact the results. Many natural questions would arise as below for this part.

What pair-wise similarity was used for clustering subgraphs? Was it that of Eq (2) ...?

What does "First, we sampled a large number of subgraphs (e.g., k-hop neighborhoods)" exactly mean? Did you use just uniformly random sampling of "k-hop neighborhoods"? How to set k? How to fix the number of samples? 

Are there any other options than k-hop neighborhoods? For example, we can use the motif vocabulary by BRICS algorithm used in MGSSL (Zhang et al, 2021). Have you ever tested it?

Did you investigate how this selection of representative subgraphs affects the final outcomes or the empirical superiority of the proposed MCM?


- One of the big limitations would be the lack of comparisons to multiple methods to take into account subgraphs or motifs directly or indirectly (other than MGSSL by Zhang et al, 2021). Subgraphs are only relevant features if only graph topology is given, and GNN research has made efforts to relate message passing to subgraphs (For example, results of 1-WL vs GNN and higher-order GNN, etc, like [1] [2] [3] to name a few). So it might be sometimes indirect, but a lot of existing research would be related to this work.

[1] Papp & Wattenhofer. A Theoretical Comparison of Graph Neural Network Extensions.
    https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.12884

[2] Morris et al. Weisfeiler and Leman Go Neural: Higher-order Graph Neural Networks (AAAI2019)
    https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.02244

[3] Bodnar et al. Weisfeiler and Lehman Go Cellular: CW Networks (NeurIPS2021)
    https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.12575

In particular, the motif vocabulary was directly sampled from the given training dataset and sounds like this vocabulary not adding any additional inductive biases into representation learning. If so, this abstract awareness

In short, proposed MCM compares each of motifs to the subgraphs center at each node. So if we stack GNN layers with an attention mechanism, this might be expected to be achieved as we see in the hierarchy of visual features in CNN architectures for images. For example, now that standard GNN packages such as PyTorch Geometric (PyG) come with multi-head attention versions of GAT and GATv2 plus ResNet like staking of GNN layers by DeepGCN or the like, and it would be appreciated to ensure somehow whether or not combining these standard established techniques are insufficient to consider motif or subgraph structures. For example, AttentiveFP [4] (available in PyG) used the stacking of edge attention message passing, and the original paper presented results showing that attention weights focused on some specific substructure motifs, such as rings. So if we stacked attention-based GNNs with multi heads, the focus on several substructural motifs as well as motif-motif interactions could also be naturally considered in standard GNNs.

[4] Xiong et al. Pushing the Boundaries of Molecular Representation for Drug Discovery with the Graph Attention Mechanism (2020)
    https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jmedchem.9b00959

In addition, the following work [5] [6] would also try to (somehow) consider motif subgraphs, and it would be nice to discuss/investigate the differences. ICML2022 was held in July, and ICLR2023 submission deadline was late September, and knowing these results would not be impossible though I can fully understand we cannot consider every related method anymore nowadays. Also, subgraph-based methods such as Graph Substructure Network (GSN) [7], one of comparing baselines in [5], might be related. For considering subgraph-subgraph attention, we can also use a stack of Transformer layers for graphs, one of the recent hot topics in GNNs (For example, as an overview is given in [8]).

[5] Yu and Gao, Molecular Representation Learning via Heterogeneous Motif Graph Neural Networks (ICML2022)
    https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00529

[6] Chen et. al, Structure-Aware Transformer for Graph Representation Learning (ICML2022)
    https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03036

[7] Bouritsas et al, Improving Graph Neural Network Expressivity via Subgraph Isomorphism Counting (TPAMI2022)
    https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.09252
    https://doi.org/10.1109/TPAMI.2022.3154319

[8] Min et al, Transformer for Graphs: An Overview from Architecture Perspective (2022)
    https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.08455

- The explainability discussed in 3.4 would be unconvincing to me. The resultant interpretation seems to come directly from t-SNE, and would not be a direct contribution of MCM. Now that we have many GNN interpretation methods, such as highly cited [9] and [10], it would need a much more detailed investigation if the paper claims interpretability or explainability.

[9] Ying et al. GNNExplainer: Generating Explanations for Graph Neural Networks (NeurIPS2019)
    https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.03894

[10] Yuan et al. Explainability in Graph Neural Networks: A Taxonomic Survey (TPAMI2022)
     https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.15445

[11] Liu, Feng, Hu, Chapter7: Interpretability in Graph Neural Networks.
    https://graph-neural-networks.github.io/gnnbook_Chapter7.html
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper's presentation is a bit redundant but readable, but also comes with a couple of unclear points, as I described above about "motif vocabulary construction." In particular, how to prepare "motif vocabulary" (including sampling strategy, types of sampled subgraphs, the choice for k, the choice for representative subgraphs, etc.) was unclear.

As far as I know, the idea of this paper is novel, and the paper also provides the codebase as supplementary materials for ensuring reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents an interesting idea of generating "already motif-aware" features at each node by similarities between prepared motifs and subgraph centered at the node and using it as initial node features of GNN learning. The empirical results demonstrated this simple worked, and it can be very powerful even without subsequent GNN layers, as specifically demonstrated for the toy small case. However, it is still unclear whether this simple method is one of the better options than combining already existing design patterns of GNNs such as stacking of attentive GNN, subgraph-based GNN, GNN transformers, etc.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
